extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A Prong Two). Focuses on considerations, procedural steps, and examples for Section 101 patent-eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application if it 'applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.' If so, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate integration using the considerations listed in the MPEP subsection I (improvements, particular treatment/prophylaxis, particular machine/manufacture, particular transformation, other meaningful uses). If the claim integrates the exception into a practical application the eligibility analysis concludes at Step 2A. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for detailed discussion and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in the functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First evaluate the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly assert the improvement, but the improvement must be apparent to a person of ordinary skill; conclusory assertions are insufficient. Next, ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement (the claim must include the components or steps that provide the improvement, though it need not expressly state the improvement). Examples: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip-sync/animation), Visual Memory (enhanced memory), Finjan (virus scanning), SRI (network monitoring). This consideration in Step 2A does not reference whether elements are routine or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not directed to the judicial exception if additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration focuses on using the exception to treat or prevent disease (e.g., administration of medication, dialysis, surgery, acupuncture, phototherapy). The Vanda case is illustrative: claims that used a genotype-based dosing regimen to reduce patient risk of QTc prolongation were eligible because the administration steps were used to treat safely, unlike Mayo where administration was ancillary to data-gathering. Evaluate whether the claimed administration/use is directed to treatment (meaningful limit) rather than diagnostic data collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing a judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration can be demonstrated when the judicial exception is implemented with, or used in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.05(b) for detailed analysis. Note that merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea or merely reciting generic machine implementation is insufficient (see negative considerations). The claim should tie the exception to a particular machine or manufacture in a way that meaningfully limits the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can demonstrate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.05(c) for examples and detailed guidance. The transformation should be meaningful and tied to the claimed invention, not merely incidental or generic physical steps that do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration is also demonstrated when the judicial exception is applied or used in a meaningful way beyond generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all for meaningful limitations that do not fit the other listed categories but still make the claim more than an attempt to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for discussion and case law examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely reciting 'apply it' or implementing on a computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent), merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation is discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(f). Examiners should treat such recitations as non-meaningful additions that do not prevent the claim from being 'directed to' the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity does not integrate the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception is not sufficient to show integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.05(g) and Parker v. Flook example where failure to explain how to select key parameters rendered additional steps insignificant post-solution activity. Examiners should look for substantive, specific steps that meaningfully use the exception rather than generic or ancillary activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking to a technological environment or field of use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(h). Claims that simply state a field-of-use or technological context without meaningful limitations are still considered directed to the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two excludes consideration of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A Prong Two, examiners should specifically exclude consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity; examiners should give weight to all additional elements whether or not they are conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Step 2B, Step 2A evaluates integration without reference to conventionality; additional elements that are well-understood, routine, or conventional may nevertheless integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. See discussion distinguishing Step 2A and Step 2B analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility or physicality is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; physical implementation alone does not guarantee eligibility, nor does a non-physical element doom eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice Corp. (physicality 'is beside the point'), Genetic Technologies (DNA steps not sufficient), Enfish and McRO (intangible improvements can be eligible). Evaluate how elements meaningfully limit the exception rather than relying on tangibility as a proxy for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether the limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims lack specifics (e.g., do not explain how to select parameters, how to perform steps, or how the steps effect the result), those limitations may be characterized as insignificant post-solution activity (see Parker v. Flook). Conversely, sufficiently specific limitations that show how the exception is used can support integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to evaluate integration (procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the listed considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluation applies equally to abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena/products of nature. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim; the analysis is not a weighing test—what matters is the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant's invention and whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception. If the claim integrates the exception based on these considerations, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and the claim is eligible at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate each claim separately; dependent claims may differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim may be ineligible while another dependent claim is eligible if the dependent claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more or that integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification support required to recognize an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that a claim demonstrates an improvement in technology, the specification should provide sufficient details such that a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing that improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not use the word 'improvement' explicitly, but must disclose sufficient detail to make the improvement apparent; bare/conclusory assertions of improvement are insufficient. After establishing specification support, ensure the claim actually reflects the improvements described in the specification (claim limitations must embody the components/steps providing the improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and case-law illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP provides numerous case examples illustrating Prong Two conclusions (e.g., Solutran, Finjan, Enfish, McRO, Vanda, BASCOM, Visual Memory, SRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these cases as guidance: Solutran (claims directed to abstract idea due to lacking technological improvement), Finjan (virus scanning found to improve computer functionality due to security profile steps), Vanda (treatment/prophylaxis eligible), Enfish/McRO/Visual Memory/SRI (examples of technological improvements). Apply factual distinctions and specification/claim analysis from cases to the facts of the application under examination.
